questions.prompt: A ringing bell is placed in a jar and the air is pumped out. What happens?
options: The sound gets fainter and finally can't be heard
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.prompt: Order from the FASTEST speed of sound to the SLOWEST.
questions.explain: Sound travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases.

questions.prompt: Why can't astronauts on a spacewalk talk to each other directly, without radios?
options: There is no air (medium) to carry sound
Sound is too slow in space

questions.prompt: You shout towards a cliff and hear the echo 2 seconds later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
questions.hint: The sound travels there AND back.

questions.prompt: You see lightning and hear the thunder 6 seconds later. About how far away was the lightning? (Speed of sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explain: Light arrives almost instantly; sound takes 6 s: 340 × 6 = 2040 m, about 2 km.

questions.prompt: When a sound wave passes through air, the air particles…
options: travel all the way from the source to your ear
vibrate back and forth around their positions, passing the vibration on
questions.explain: The vibration travels; the particles only jiggle about their places.

questions.prompt: Why is there no echo in a small, furnished bedroom?
options: The reflected sound returns in less than 0.1 s and merges with the original sound
questions.explain: You need to be at least about 17 m from the reflecting surface to hear a separate echo; soft furnishings also absorb sound.

questions.prompt: Explain, using particles, why sound travels faster in steel than in air.
questions.modelAnswer: In steel, the particles are packed very closely and strongly bonded to their neighbours, so when one particle vibrates it passes the vibration on almost immediately. In air, the particles are far apart and only pass on the vibration when they collide, so the vibration travels more slowly.
rubric: Particles far apart in gases, so slower
questions.explain: Link the particle model to the speed of sound.
